title: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson
author: Mark Twain
written: 1892-93, at Florence, out of a farce about Siamese twins that Twain cut in half
setting: Dawson’s Landing, a slaveholding town on the Missouri bank of the Mississippi, half a day below St Louis, between 1830 and 1853
lengthNote: Twenty-one chapters and a conclusion, about 55,000 words, each chapter opening with a motto from Pudd’nhead Wilson’s calendar
openingLine: The scene of this chronicle is the town of Dawson’s Landing, on the Missouri side of the Mississippi, half a day’s journey, per steamboat, below St. Louis.
summary: A slave called Roxy, who is one-sixteenth black and looks white, swaps her baby for her master’s to keep her son from being sold down the river. The two boys grow up in each other’s places: hers becomes the petted heir, the master’s son becomes a servant who cannot read. Twenty-three years later a murder brings the case to court, and a lawyer nobody in the town has ever taken seriously wins it with fingerprints. The book is often funny and never comfortable: everything that decides who these people are turns out to be paperwork.
referenceStyle: chapter number, following the 1894 American text

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (eBook 102)
sourceText.note: The 1894 American text, with Twain’s spellings and the dialect as he wrote it. The novel repeatedly uses a racial slur, which is not reproduced in the quotations here.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Begun in Florence as a farce about conjoined twins, then cut apart: the twins were separated and the changeling plot took over.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Serialised in The Century Magazine from December 1893, then published as a book in 1894 with Those Extraordinary Twins printed after it.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Each opens with a motto from the calendar of a man the town thinks is a fool.

atAGlance.label: Setting
atAGlance.note: Dawson's Landing, a fictional slaveholding town on the Missouri side of the Mississippi.

structure.label: Chapters I-II
structure.title: A town, a joke, and a threat
structure.summary: Twain builds the town before he builds the plot: rose-vines, cats on window-sills, the first families of Virginia, and the slave market a steamboat ride downstream. A young lawyer arrives, makes a remark about half a dog, and is written off for twenty years. In the second chapter a theft among the house slaves is punished with a threat that sets the whole novel moving.

scenes.title: Pudd'nhead wins his name
scenes.summary: David Wilson says he would kill his half of a barking dog. The town decides he is a fool, and his legal career is over before it starts.

scenes.title: The first families
scenes.summary: Judge Driscoll, Pembroke Howard and Colonel Essex: the Virginian code of honour, transplanted to a river town and taken entirely seriously.

scenes.title: Driscoll spares his slaves
scenes.summary: Percy Driscoll threatens to sell the thieves down the river, then contents himself with selling them locally and congratulates himself on his mercy.

scenes.title: Roxy and the two babies
scenes.summary: Roxy, white to look at and a slave in law, is nursing her master's son and her own, born within weeks of each other.

structure.label: Chapters III-IV
structure.title: Roxy plays a shrewd trick
structure.summary: Terrified that her son can be sold, Roxy dresses him in the other baby's ruffles and puts the master's child in the tow-linen shirt. Nobody notices, which is the point: the difference the town would kill for is laundry. The chapter of aftermath watches the two children grow into the roles the cradle gave them, one insufferable, the other beaten into service.

scenes.title: The cradle
scenes.summary: Roxy tries on the change as an experiment, sees that even she cannot tell them apart, and keeps it.

scenes.title: The finger-prints
scenes.summary: Wilson has been taking impressions of the town's fingers as a hobby for years, including the children's, and files them away.

scenes.title: The ways of the changelings
scenes.summary: Tom grows up spoiled and cruel; Chambers becomes his protector, his swimming champion and his whipping boy.

scenes.title: Roxy's position
scenes.summary: Freed at Percy Driscoll's death, she goes to work on the river boats and leaves her son to the inheritance she stole for him.

structure.label: Chapters V-XI
structure.title: Two Italians, and a hobby nobody respects
structure.summary: The Capello twins take lodgings in the town and are received as a sensation. Tom, back from Yale and deeper in debt than anyone knows, insults Luigi, is kicked across a stage in front of the town, and then will not fight the duel his uncle’s code requires. Through all of it Wilson keeps taking finger-prints, and the town keeps finding it comic.

scenes.title: The twins thrill Dawson's Landing
scenes.summary: Angelo and Luigi arrive, play the piano four-handed, and are inspected by the whole town at Aunt Patsy's.

scenes.title: The unknown nymph
scenes.summary: Tom's thefts have begun; a girl in the window of Judge Driscoll's house is seen, and is not a girl.

scenes.title: Marse Tom tramples his chance
scenes.summary: Roxy returns, penniless, to ask her son for help, and is refused with contempt.

scenes.title: Pudd'nhead's startling discovery
scenes.summary: Wilson takes Tom's prints and finds a record that does not fit, though he cannot yet say why.

structure.label: Chapters XII-XVIII
structure.title: What Roxy knows
structure.summary: Roxy tells her son what he is, and the balance of power in the book turns over: the heir is a slave in law, the slave is his mother, and she can hang him with a sentence. She takes half his allowance, orders him to reform, and when he sells her down the river to clear his debts she comes back up it to make her terms plainer.

scenes.title: The shame of Judge Driscoll
scenes.summary: The refused duel disgraces the family; the Judge fights it himself, at sixty, because the code allows nothing else.

scenes.title: Roxana insists upon reform
scenes.summary: She takes charge of her son's conduct and his money, and he obeys because the alternative is being sold.

scenes.title: Sold down the river
scenes.summary: Tom sells his own mother to an Arkansas cotton planter and tells himself it is temporary.

scenes.title: Roxana commands
scenes.summary: Escaped and back in the town, she gives him one instruction: get the money from his uncle, whatever it takes.

structure.label: Chapters XIX-Conclusion
structure.title: A knife, a courtroom, and two men in the wrong lives
structure.summary: Tom robs his uncle in disguise, kills him with the twins' Indian knife, and the town arrests the foreigners. Wilson, defending them, finds a bloody thumb-print on the haft, matches it to a record in his files, and in doing so discovers the exchange of 1830. The last page disposes of both men as property: one unfit for the drawing room, the other worth too much to be imprisoned.

scenes.title: The prophecy realized
scenes.summary: The Judge is stabbed in his own house by a figure in women's clothes.

scenes.title: The murderer chuckles
scenes.summary: Tom watches the twins charged with his crime and enjoys it.

scenes.title: Doom
scenes.summary: Wilson’s courtroom demonstration: the natal autograph, the glass strips, and the sentence that names the murderer and the changeling together.

scenes.title: What became of them
scenes.summary: Chambers cannot use the life he is given back; Roxy's spirit is broken; and the state, having pardoned a murderer, sells him to pay the estate's debts.

characters.name: Roxana
characters.role: A slave in the Driscoll house, and the mother of the boy raised as Tom
characters.summary: Handsome, quick and twenty, with a manner that changes the moment a white person is in the room. She commits the novel's central act out of terror and then has to live inside it for twenty-three years, first as a servant to her own son, then as his creditor, and finally as the person he sells. She is the only character in the book who acts; the rest drift.
characters.clue: One sixteenth black, white to look at, and the most formidable person in Dawson's Landing.
traits: unsentimental about the world she is in

relationships.label: mother of, servant to, then blackmailer of

characters.name: Tom Driscoll
characters.role: Roxy's son, put in the heir's cradle at seven months old
characters.summary: Petted, cowardly and cruel from childhood, a gambler by twenty and a thief by twenty-three. Twain does not put his badness down to his blood, or to his upbringing alone: he is what unchecked indulgence plus a family fortune plus a terror of exposure produces, and the novel leaves the causes visible and unsorted.
characters.clue: Born Valet de Chambre, and does not learn it until his mother tells him at twenty-three.

relationships.label: son of, and owner of on paper
nephew and heir of, then murderer of

characters.name: Chambers
characters.role: Percy Driscoll's son, raised as a slave
characters.summary: Strong, kind and entirely powerless. He takes the beatings meant for the other boy, saves him from drowning, and is thanked with contempt. When the exchange is undone he is twenty-three, cannot read, speaks the dialect of the kitchen, and is at home in neither the parlour nor the place he has been turned out of.
characters.clue: Freed into a life he has no training for, and comfortable only where he is no longer allowed to sit.

relationships.label: servant to, and the man whose life he has

characters.name: David Wilson
characters.role: A lawyer with no practice, called Pudd'nhead for twenty years
characters.summary: An educated outsider whose one joke is taken literally, after which the town files him under harmless. He surveys, keeps accounts, collects finger-prints and writes a calendar of aphorisms nobody reads. The plot turns when his hobby becomes evidence, and his reward is to be elected mayor by the people who could not follow his joke.
characters.clue: Says he would kill his half of a dog, and waits twenty-three years to be taken seriously.

relationships.label: files his prints, then convicts him
friend of, in the Freethinkers' Society

characters.name: Judge York Leicester Driscoll
characters.role: Percy's brother, Tom's uncle, and the town's first citizen
characters.summary: A Virginian gentleman of the old school, an unbeliever in private and a stickler for the code in public. The duel he fights at sixty and the will he tears up twice are both matters of honour, and the code that requires them leaves him alone in a house with an unarmed nephew.
characters.clue: Tears up his will when his nephew will not fight, and writes it again when he thinks better of him.

characters.name: Percy Northumberland Driscoll
characters.summary: A land speculator who considers himself a humane master because he sells his thieving slaves inside the state, not down the river, and records the act in his diary as mercy. He never discovers the exchange, and dies believing the boy in the ruffles is his son.
characters.clue: Congratulates himself in his diary on a merciful day's work.

relationships.label: father of, without knowing it after the switch

characters.name: Luigi Capello
characters.role: One of the Italian twins, and the man accused of the murder
characters.summary: The darker, quicker-tempered brother, who has killed a man before and says so. His kick at Tom is the most popular act in the town's recent history and the start of Tom's ruin; his knife, stolen, becomes the murder weapon and the evidence against him.
characters.clue: Kicks a coward off a stage in front of the whole town and is elected to the council for it.

characters.name: Angelo Capello
characters.role: The fairer twin, a teetotaller and a churchgoer
characters.summary: Mild where his brother is fierce, and treated by the town as half of one curiosity, not as a person. The pair are the remains of the conjoined-twin farce Twain cut out of the book, and what survives of that joke is a running question about how much of anyone's character is their own.
characters.clue: Signs the pledge while his brother drinks, and is arrested alongside him anyway.

characters.name: Pembroke Howard
characters.role: Lawyer, Virginian, and the Judge's second
characters.summary: The keeper of the code in a town that has half forgotten why it has one. He arranges the duel, prosecutes the twins for the murder of his friend, and never once doubts that the rules he grew up with are the same thing as justice.
characters.clue: Arranges a duel and a prosecution with the same unhurried correctness.

themes.name: A fraction, and what it decides
themes.summary: Roxy is white to look at and a slave in law; her son is thirty-one parts white and salable. The novel states the arithmetic flatly and then spends twenty-one chapters showing that nobody in the town can see the difference it supposedly marks.
themes.development: The first statement is an authorial aside in chapter three; by the courtroom it has become the sentence that disposes of two grown men, and the last page prices one of them.

themes.name: Two cradles, two lives
themes.summary: Everything the town treats as character — bearing, speech, courage, gentility — is handed out in chapter three along with the ruffled muslin. The experiment runs for twenty-three years and neither the family nor the reader can point to the moment a nature asserted itself.
themes.development: The exchange is undone in a courtroom, but the training cannot be: Chambers is given his name and his money and can use neither.

themes.name: What made Tom
themes.summary: Twain keeps two explanations in play and does not choose between them. Tom is indulged from birth, terrified of exposure from twenty-three, and the narration occasionally floats a third suggestion about blood — then gives the evidence against it.
themes.development: Roxy blames the fraction in him; Tom blames his birth; the book shows a household that would have produced a bully out of anybody.

themes.name: Law, evidence and property
themes.summary: The trial is a triumph of method: a new kind of proof, presented by the one man in town who has been doing science instead of gossip. It convicts a murderer, corrects a twenty-three-year deception, and delivers both men to the market.
themes.development: Wilson's finger-prints answer the question of who did it and cannot touch the question the book actually raises, which is who these people were allowed to be.

themes.name: The code of the first families
themes.summary: Dawson's Landing runs on a Virginian honour system: duels, wills torn up and rewritten, an insult settled with pistols at sixty. It is treated with perfect seriousness by everyone in the town and as a farce by the man telling the story.
themes.development: The refused duel disgraces Tom before the town knows anything worse about him, and the Judge's willingness to fight leaves him alone in the house with his heir.

themes.name: Debt, allowance and a town's opinion
themes.summary: Money runs under every plot turn: a gambling debt sets the thefts going, an allowance gives Roxy her hold, and an estate's creditors decide the ending. Reputation is the other currency, and Wilson spends twenty years without any.
themes.development: The town's verdict on a man — fool, gentleman, foreigner — is shown to be as arbitrary as the cradle, and as binding.

themes.name: A joke that lasts twenty years
themes.summary: One remark about a dog is taken literally and costs Wilson his profession. The town's certainty that he is a fool is the same faculty that lets it believe Tom is a Driscoll, and the novel lets the two errors correct together.
themes.development: His calendar mocks the town from the head of every chapter; the town elects him mayor the moment he does something it can understand.

techniques.name: The calendar mottoes
techniques.definition: An aphorism at the head of each chapter, attributed to a character inside the book.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilson's calendar is the novel's second voice: dry, bleak and usually about human self-deception. The entries are funny on their own and pointed in place — the April Fool motto stands over the chapter in which the trial begins.

techniques.name: Speech as evidence
techniques.definition: Writing characters' pronunciation and idiom as they are heard.
techniques.inThisBook: Roxy's speech and Chambers's are the same dialect, and one of them is the son of the house. The novel makes that audible before it makes it explicit, so the reader hears the training that the town mistakes for nature.

techniques.name: The narrator's straight face
techniques.definition: Reporting something outrageous in the tone used for the ordinary.
techniques.inThisBook: Percy Driscoll congratulates himself on a merciful day's work after threatening to sell four people down the river, and the narration records the self-congratulation without comment. The technique is Twain's whole method here.

techniques.name: Pairs that cannot be told apart
techniques.definition: Two figures set up as a matched pair so the differences between them can be examined.
techniques.inThisBook: Two babies, two young men, two Italian twins, and a lawyer's hobby that exists to tell identical things apart. The twins are what survived when Twain cut a farce about conjoined brothers out of the manuscript.

techniques.name: The courtroom demonstration
techniques.definition: An extended public scene in which the plot is resolved in front of an audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilson lectures a packed court on the natal autograph, pauses until the room goes quiet, and then names the murderer. The scene is a magic act, and Twain gives it every beat of one.

techniques.name: Threats that come true
techniques.definition: A line planted early that the plot later carries out.
techniques.inThisBook: Being sold down the river is a threat in chapter two, a terror in chapter three, an act in chapter sixteen and the last five words of the book.

techniques.name: Glass strips and an Indian knife
techniques.definition: Physical things that carry the plot and the argument together.
techniques.inThisBook: The knife passes from the twins to Tom and back as evidence; the glass strips hold twenty years of the town's fingers. Both are objects that can say who a person is when no one in the town can.

quotations.text: I wish I owned half of that dog.
quotations.context: David Wilson, newly arrived, listening to an invisible dog bark.
quotations.analysis: The joke needs its second half — he would kill his half — and the town cannot supply it. A man's whole career is decided in the four seconds it takes them to fail at a syllogism, which is the same failure that will let them accept a changed baby.

quotations.text: Because I would kill my half.
quotations.context: Wilson's answer when somebody asks why.
quotations.analysis: A logician's joke about indivisible property, offered to a town whose entire economy rests on dividing people into parts. Twain sets the terms of the book in a throwaway line: a fraction of a living thing cannot be owned separately, and the law says otherwise.

quotations.text: You ought to be sold down the river.
quotations.context: Percy Driscoll, having decided to sell his four thieving slaves locally instead.
quotations.analysis: The sentence that starts the plot. It is spoken as mercy, received as mercy, and written down that night in his diary as a humane day's work — and it is what sends Roxy to the cradle three chapters later.

quotations.text: To all intents and purposes Roxy was as white as anybody, but the one sixteenth of her which was black outvoted the other fifteen parts and made her a negro.
quotations.analysis: 'Outvoted' is the whole argument in one word: the classification is a procedure, not a fact, and a minority of the arithmetic wins because the rules were written that way. Twain states it without heat, in the voice of a man reading out a regulation.

quotations.text: Her child was thirty-one parts white, and he, too, was a slave, and by a fiction of law and custom a negro.
quotations.context: The same passage, moving from mother to son.
quotations.analysis: A fiction is what lawyers call a thing everyone agrees to treat as true. Twain uses the technical sense and the ordinary one together, and the sentence lets the reader know that the machinery about to run for twenty-three years is made of paper.

quotations.text: Adam was but human—this explains it all. He did not want the apple for the apple’s sake, he wanted it only because it was forbidden.
quotations.context: The motto at the head of the chapter in which Driscoll's slaves steal.
quotations.analysis: Placed above a theft, the aphorism undercuts the moral the chapter seems to offer. The people who stole are not wicked; they are human beings in a house where everything is forbidden them, and the calendar says so before the narrative does.
quotations.source: 1894 text, calendar motto to chapter II

quotations.text: Whoever has lived long enough to find out what life is, knows how deep a debt of gratitude we owe to Adam, the first great benefactor of our race. He brought death into the world.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter in which Roxy contemplates drowning herself and her child.
quotations.analysis: The bleakest joke in the calendar, standing over the chapter where a mother works out that death is better than the auction block. The aphorism arrives as wit and is then taken literally by the plot beneath it.
quotations.source: 1894 text, calendar motto to chapter III

quotations.context: Roxy at the cradle in the night, after learning her child can be sold.
quotations.analysis: The sentence breaks before it finishes. Everything Roxy does for the rest of the novel — the switch, the blackmail, the escape from Arkansas — is contained in a half-spoken refusal muttered over a cot at two in the morning.

quotations.text: It ain’t no lie, nuther. It’s jes de truth, en nothin’ but de truth, so he’p me. Yassir—you’s my son—
quotations.context: Roxy telling Tom what she did in 1830.
quotations.analysis: She swears it in the language of a courtroom oath, thirteen chapters before the courtroom. The revelation is also a transfer of power: from this line on the woman he has just refused a dollar can hang him with a sentence, and both of them know it.

quotations.text: If you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous, he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter called Sold Down the River.
quotations.analysis: The chapter beneath it has a son selling his mother to a cotton planter after she has saved him twice. The calendar's dog returns from chapter one, and the joke that once cost Wilson his practice now measures Tom exactly.
quotations.source: 1894 text, calendar motto to chapter XVI

quotations.text: April 1. This is the day upon which we are reminded of what we are on the other three hundred and sixty-four.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter of the trial.
quotations.analysis: Over a courtroom, the joke becomes a verdict on everybody in it: a town that has been fooled for twenty-three years is about to be told so, and the man who wrote the line is the one doing the telling.
quotations.source: 1894 text, calendar motto to chapter XXI

quotations.text: These marks are his signature, his physiological autograph, so to speak, and this autograph can not be counterfeited
quotations.context: Wilson explaining finger-prints to a court that has never heard of them.
quotations.analysis: A signature nobody can forge, in a book where every other kind of identity — a name, a will, a family, a race — turns out to be forgeable. The science arrives as a relief and settles the wrong question, which is Twain's joke on the ending.

quotations.text: Upon this haft stands the assassin’s natal autograph, written in the blood of that helpless and unoffending old man who loved you and whom you all loved.
quotations.context: Wilson, holding the knife in front of the jury.
quotations.analysis: The rhetoric is pure theatre — the pause, the raised eyes, the clock — and it works because the town has spent twenty years underestimating the man performing it. Twain gives his outsider the one scene in which a Dawson's Landing audience listens.

quotations.text: make upon the window the finger-prints that will hang you!
quotations.context: The end of Wilson's demonstration, addressed across the courtroom.
quotations.analysis: The order is to produce the evidence himself, in public, and he obeys by fainting. Two secrets are settled in one sentence: who killed the Judge, and who has been living in the Driscoll house since 1830.

quotations.text: The poor fellow could not endure the terrors of the white man’s parlor, and felt at home and at peace nowhere but in the kitchen.
quotations.context: What becomes of the real heir once he has his name and his money back.
quotations.analysis: The restoration is a formality. Twenty-three years of training cannot be reversed by a verdict, and the novel's coldest sentence shows a free man with an estate who is comfortable only where he used to be sent.

quotations.text: the spirit in her eye was quenched
quotations.analysis: The most vital character in the book is dismissed in half a line. Twain gives her the courage, the plan and the nerve for twenty-one chapters and then records, without ceremony, that the ending has taken all of it away.

quotations.text: As soon as the Governor understood the case, he pardoned Tom at once, and the creditors sold him down the river.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: A murderer is pardoned because imprisoning him would waste an asset, and the estate's creditors take him instead. The threat from chapter two arrives as the final clause of the book, and the law that has just performed a miracle of detection hands a man over as goods.

quotations.text: Tell the truth or trump--but get the trick.
quotations.context: The first motto in the book, above the chapter that names Wilson.
quotations.analysis: This is a card-player's morality, and the working rule of nearly everyone in Dawson's Landing. It also describes the trial: Wilson tells the truth and takes the trick, and the town cannot tell the two apart.
quotations.source: 1894 text, calendar motto to chapter I

timeline.label: The novel's opening: Roxy switches the babies in 1830
timeline.detail: Roxy changes the two babies in the Driscoll nursery; both are about seven months old.

timeline.label: Clemens's boyhood in Hannibal, Missouri
timeline.detail: Hannibal, Missouri, where Samuel Clemens grew up watching slaves shipped south, is the model for Dawson's Landing.

timeline.label: The novel's murder trial, set in 1853
timeline.detail: The murder of Judge Driscoll and Wilson's finger-print demonstration close the novel's action.

timeline.label: Faulds and Herschel argue for finger-prints
timeline.detail: Letters in Nature propose using finger-prints for identification, a decade before Twain wrote the trial.

timeline.label: Galton's Finger Prints published
timeline.detail: Francis Galton's book established that the patterns are unique and unchanging; Twain read about the method while the novel was in progress.

timeline.label: Begun as a farce
timeline.detail: Twain started a comic story about conjoined twins in Florence, then found the changeling plot taking it over.

timeline.label: Twain cuts the Siamese twins out of the novel
timeline.detail: He separated the brothers, pulled their story out as Those Extraordinary Twins, and rewrote what remained.

timeline.label: Serialised in The Century
timeline.detail: The novel ran in The Century Magazine from December 1893 to June 1894, with illustrations.

timeline.label: Published as a book
timeline.detail: The American Publishing Company issued it with Those Extraordinary Twins appended and Twain's note explaining the surgery.

timeline.label: Plessy v. Ferguson
timeline.detail: Two years after publication the Supreme Court upheld segregation in a case turning on a man who was seven-eighths white.

timeline.label: Leslie Fiedler's defence
timeline.detail: Fiedler called the novel a great and neglected American book, and modern criticism of it effectively starts here.

places.name: Hannibal, Missouri
places.note: Twain's boyhood town on the Mississippi, and the original of Dawson's Landing.

places.name: St Louis, Missouri
places.note: Half a day upstream by steamboat; where Tom gambles and pawns what he steals.

places.name: New Orleans, Louisiana
places.note: The end of the river, and what 'sold down the river' means in practice.

places.name: The Arkansas cotton country
places.note: Where Tom sells his mother, and where she is worked in the fields before she escapes.

places.name: Florence, Italy
places.note: Where Twain wrote the book, in the winter of 1892-93.

criticalViews.summary: The novel treats racial category as an administrative fiction and shows it deciding everything, which makes it more radical than Huckleberry Finn's moral drama of one boy's conscience.
criticalViews.counter: It also gives its villain a fraction of black ancestry and lets characters attribute his conduct to it. Whether Twain is quoting that belief or sharing it is the argument the book has never settled.

criticalViews.position: A detective story with the wrong ending
criticalViews.summary: The finger-print trial is the first courtroom use of the method in fiction, and it works: the case is solved, the innocent freed, the imposture exposed.
criticalViews.counter: The solution restores a system the book has spent twenty chapters discrediting. The court proves who everybody is and then prices them, which reads less like a resolution than a demonstration.

criticalViews.position: A book that shows its own seams
criticalViews.summary: Twain admitted he cut a farce in half to make it, and the twins, the duel and the tangled last chapters are what is left of the surgery.
criticalViews.counter: The seams do work: the twins are the book's second pair of interchangeable men, and a novel about people who cannot be told apart is not damaged by having been built out of two stories nobody could separate.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the novel present identity as something the town decides, and not something people have?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, training and the fiction of law
plan: Start with the passage of arithmetic in chapter two: outvoted, and a fiction of law and custom.
Use the exchange itself — muslin and tow-linen, and a mother who cannot tell them apart by sight.
Follow the training: Tom's cruelty and cowardice, Chambers's dialect and deference, both fully formed by adolescence.
Set the courtroom against the conclusion: the verdict corrects the record and cannot correct the men.
Weigh the narrator's occasional hints about blood, and decide whether the book endorses them or records them.

essayQuestions.question: What is the calendar for?
essayQuestions.focus: The epigraphs as the novel's second voice
plan: Establish the device: a motto at the head of every chapter, by a character inside the story.
Read three in their places — Adam and the apple above a theft, the starving dog above a sale, April Fool above the trial.
Consider the tone: bleak, aphoristic, and quite unlike the narration around it.
Ask what it means that the wisest voice in the book belongs to the man the town calls a fool.
Conclude on whether the calendar comments on the plot or judges the reader.

essayQuestions.question: Is Roxy the novel's hero?
plan: Set out what she does: the switch, the return, the revelation, the terms she imposes, the escape from Arkansas.
Weigh the moral position: she saves her child by condemning another woman's to slavery, and knows it.
Examine her speech, and what the novel does by giving the most intelligent plan in the book to the kitchen dialect.
Consider her treatment by the plot: sold by her own son, then dismissed in half a sentence at the end.
Decide whether the ending is Twain's judgement on her or his account of what the system does to her.

essayQuestions.question: Does the trial resolve the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, justice and what a court can settle
plan: Describe the demonstration: the physiological autograph, the glass records, the pause before the naming.
Note what it establishes — a murderer, an imposture, two true names.
Note what it leaves untouched: the law that made the switch worth making.
Take the final sentence as the test: a pardon granted because a man is property.
Argue whether the detective ending is a failure of nerve or the book's last piece of irony.
